newsitem.title: CHINA: China curbs burials, promotes cremation.
newsitem.headline: China curbs burials, promotes cremation.

text.p: China has tightened regulations to curb traditional burials and promote cremation to try to save precious arable land and stamp out extravagant funeral ceremonies, officials said on Wednesday.
"The regulations were issued because of the lack of integrated burial management in China," a Ministry of Civil Affairs official said.
"In some areas, people bury dead bodies where they like and in other areas feudal superstitions have revived," he said. He gave no details of the superstitious practices.
However, under the new regulations passed by the State Council, or cabinet, cremation would become the standard practice in densely populated areas, the official China Daily said.

The rules ban tombs or graves on arable and forest land, in city parks, tourist spots, along river banks and railways and highways, the newspaper quoted Yang Yanyin, vice-minister of civil affairs, as saying.
Burial would still be allowed in areas without crematoria and the rules would not interfere with the funerary customs of China's ethnic minorities, Yang said.

The rules aimed to "encourage people to adopt civilised interment methods such as cremation instead of outdated burial practices that occupy valuable arable land and involve expensive and superstitious ceremonies", he was quoted as saying.
Penalties would be imposed on illicit cemeteries and manufacturers or sellers of superstitious funeral products, Yang said.
China's communist authorities frown on many traditional customs as outdated superstitious practices.
Under the new rules, death certificates from the police or hospital authorities would be required before cremation to prevent criminals from destroying evidence, Yang said.

China's communist rulers have long encouraged people to cremate their dead as they struggle to preserve precious cropland and to feed 22 percent of the world's population on just seven percent of its arable land.

Many Chinese prefer to bury their dead because of a traditional belief that a body must be whole to ensure an afterlife and in recent years have increasingly defied government campaigns to stamp out "feudal" practices such as making offerings of money or food to the dead.
